faq: What does it mean to stitch website, Blinkit and Swiggy data?

Joining sales of the same product across channels that never share a customer identifier. It sounds like one job. It's really three — a clean key join, a rollup, and an estimate — and they are not equally trustworthy, so you have to know which one you're doing before you report from it.
What is a SKU mapping table?

One table that says your 250ml electrolyte bottle is this name on your site, that name on Blinkit, another on Swiggy Instamart and another on Amazon — with one canonical ID. Four platforms, four names, one physical bottle. Build this before you build a single pipeline; it's where most stitching projects stall.
What are the three tiers of stitch?

Tier 1 is deterministic: joins on keys that mean exactly the same thing on both sides — SKU, date, city, order ID within one system. The other two tiers are rollups and estimates. Keep them separate and label anything that isn't Tier 1, because mixing them is what ruins a cross-channel dashboard.
Why don't quick commerce numbers match my backend?

Gross versus net, most often. Quick commerce platforms report sell-out — units that left the dark store. Your backend reports net of returns and cancellations. Comparing the two without adjusting makes the platform look better than it is.
Can I join on pincode or customer name?

Not as Tier 1. Pincode rollups and name matching are estimates, and they belong in a labelled tier of their own. Join only on shared exact keys — SKU, date, city, channel — and mark everything else as an estimate.

The mapping table. List every SKU, write down what it's called on each platform, pick one canonical ID. Then reconcile the basics once — gross versus net, timezones, currency — before you trust anything downstream.
